title: Classroom Assessment Methods
summary: Learn to assess learning well: purposes of assessment, everyday formative techniques, test blueprints and good questions, marking with rubrics and moderation, analysing results with item statistics, and validity, reliability and fairness.
audience: Teachers, lecturers, trainers and education students

body.p: Assessment is gathering evidence of what learners know and can do, and using it to make decisions. It is not only tests: questions, observations, conversations, projects and homework are all assessment.

list: Assessment for learning (formative): finding out where learners are so teaching and learning can be adjusted.
Assessment of learning (summative): judging achievement at the end of a unit, term or course for grades, reports or certificates.
Assessment as learning: learners assess their own and each other's work, building understanding of quality and independence.
Diagnostic assessment: identifying specific strengths and gaps, often before teaching a topic.

body.p: Formative assessment, used well, is one of the most effective ways to raise achievement, because it closes the gap between what was taught and what was learned while there is still time to act.

body.tip: For every assessment, ask: what decision will I make with this information? If the answer is none, rethink the task.

body.p: Quick, frequent checks show what the whole class understands, not only the confident learners who answer first.

list: No-hands-up questioning with random selection, so everyone thinks.
Mini whiteboards or paper slates: all learners show answers at once.
Hinge questions: a carefully chosen multiple-choice question at a key point; the wrong options reveal specific misconceptions.
Exit tickets: one or two questions at the end of a lesson to plan the next one.
Think-pair-share before whole-class discussion.
Traffic lights or thumbs to signal confidence, followed up with evidence.

body.p: If 7 of 10 sampled exit tickets (70%) show a misconception, reteach it differently to the class; if only a few do, support those learners in a small group while others extend their learning. The value lies in the response, not the check itself.

body.tip: Design wrong answer options from real errors learners make; they turn a question into a diagnostic tool.

body.p: A test should sample the curriculum fairly and measure what it claims to measure. Start with a blueprint (table of specifications) that maps marks to topics and levels of thinking.

For a 50-mark test, you might allocate 40% to knowledge and understanding (20 marks), 40% to application (20 marks) and 20% to analysis and problem-solving (10 marks), spread across the topics in proportion to the time spent teaching them.

list: Use clear, simple language so reading ability does not block learners from showing subject knowledge.
Ask one thing per question.
In multiple-choice items, make every option plausible, avoid "all of the above" and keep options similar in length.
Set marks to match the effort needed, and say how many marks each question carries.
For extended tasks, give clear instructions and success criteria.
Use realistic, culturally familiar contexts.

body.tip: Ask a colleague to take your test before learners do; they will catch ambiguous questions and errors.

body.p: Consistent marking makes results fair and meaningful.

list: Prepare a marking memo or scheme listing acceptable answers and how marks are awarded, including method marks.
For extended work, use rubrics that describe performance levels for each criterion (for example, argument, evidence and organisation, each from beginning to excellent).
Mark question by question across all scripts rather than script by script, to stay consistent.
Moderate: colleagues mark a sample of each other's scripts and resolve differences.
Avoid bias: mark anonymously where possible, and ignore handwriting and names.

body.p: Comments that tell learners what to do next are more useful than grades alone. Research suggests that grades given with comments can lead learners to focus on the grade; some teachers give comments first and grades later. Good feedback is specific, timely, linked to criteria and followed by time to act on it.

body.tip: Use "two stars and a wish": two specific strengths and one specific improvement.

body.p: Simple analysis turns marks into information for teaching.

Marks of 45, 52, 58, 61, 61, 67, 70, 74, 80 and 92 have a mean of 66, a median of 64 and a mode of 61. Comparing the class mean with previous tests or other classes shows trends; the spread shows how varied achievement is.

list: Facility (difficulty) index: the proportion answering an item correctly. If 18 of 30 learners get it right, p = 0.6. Very low values show a hard item or a topic not learned.

Discrimination: compare strong and weak learners. If 9 of the top 10 but only 3 of the bottom 10 answer correctly, discrimination = 0.9 - 0.3 = 0.6, a good item. Items where weaker learners do as well as or better than stronger ones may be flawed.
Distractor analysis: if 5 of 30 learners (about 17%) choose the same wrong option, investigate the misconception behind it.

body.tip: Use item analysis to fix both teaching (re-teach weak topics) and the test (rewrite poor questions).

body.p: Good assessments are valid, reliable and fair.

list: Validity: does the assessment measure what it claims to? A spelling test is not a valid measure of creative writing; a practical task better assesses lab skills than a written test.
Reliability: would results be consistent with different markers, occasions or question versions? Clear memos, rubrics and moderation improve reliability.

Fairness: all learners have an equal opportunity to show what they know. Remove unnecessary language difficulty and cultural bias, and provide accommodations such as extra time or large print for learners who need them.
Practicality: the assessment fits the time, cost and resources available.

body.p: Prevent cheating through secure papers, varied versions, supervision and tasks that require personal or in-class work. Respond to suspected malpractice with clear, fair procedures. In the age of AI tools, include some supervised, oral or process-based assessment.

body.tip: Report results with care: describe what learners can do and their next steps, not just a number.

quiz.q: Assessment for learning is also called:
An end-of-year exam for a certificate is:

options: A short check at the end of a lesson to plan the next one
All learners show answers at once

quiz.q: In a 50-mark test with 20% for analysis, how many marks is that?

options: Make the correct answer the longest
Colleagues check samples of marking for consistency

quiz.q: 18 of 30 learners answer an item correctly. Its facility index is:
9 of the top 10 and 3 of the bottom 10 answer correctly. Discrimination is:

options: Measures what it claims to measure

quiz.q: Consistent results with different markers show good:
Extra time for a learner with dyslexia supports:
